prompt: At 1000 samples per second, equal-amplitude zero-phase cosines at 700 Hz and 300 Hz produce identical samples. You receive only the stored samples. What can you conclude?

options.text: The original tone must have been 300 Hz
options.explanation: The 700 Hz input is another possible source of exactly the same samples.

options.text: The samples alone cannot choose between those inputs
options.explanation: Correct. Aliasing makes different continuous inputs indistinguishable from their sampled values alone.

options.text: A longer analysis of these same values must reveal 700 Hz
options.explanation: More computation cannot distinguish inputs that produced the same information. Extra knowledge about acquisition would be needed.

workedExample:
1. The question gives two inputs with identical samples.
2. Any analysis using only those samples sees the same values for either input.
3. Acquisition constraints, such as a suitable input filter, can exclude the high-frequency possibility; the bare record cannot.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

prompt: A signal may contain an arbitrary-phase sinusoid at exactly 500 Hz. Is sampling at exactly 1000 samples per second sufficient under this lesson’s condition?

options.text: Yes, two samples per cycle always preserve it
options.explanation: At the endpoint a zero-phase sine is sampled only at its zeros.

options.text: Yes, if a digital filter is applied afterwards
options.explanation: Post-sampling filtering cannot restore information already lost.

options.text: No; exceed 1000 and allow a practical filter margin
options.explanation: Correct. The strict condition excludes the endpoint; real filtering needs a transition margin too.

workedExample:
1. Half the proposed rate is exactly 500 Hz.
2. An arbitrary-phase signal includes a zero-phase sine at that frequency.
3. Its samples can all be zero, so the endpoint does not preserve arbitrary amplitude and phase. Choose a higher rate with suitable input filtering.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

prompt: A 700 Hz interferer has already folded onto a wanted 300 Hz signal at 1000 samples per second. Which actions address this? Select all that apply.

options.text: On future captures, filter the analogue input before sampling
options.explanation: Correct. Reducing the interferer before sampling prevents this fold from contaminating the wanted band.

options.text: Separate the two original tones perfectly using only a 300 Hz digital notch
options.explanation: A notch removes their combined 300 Hz contribution; it cannot distinguish the originals.

options.text: On future captures, use a sufficiently higher rate with appropriate input filtering
options.explanation: Correct. A changed acquisition design can avoid this particular fold.

workedExample:
1. The stored samples contain a combined contribution at the same apparent frequency.
2. A later filter acts on that combination.
3. Prevention changes what reaches the sampler or changes the sampling design; it cannot retroactively identify the two contributions.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP
